Calculus is the study of rate of change. The functions you learn algebra (linear, polynomials, logarithmic, exponential, trigonometric) are of the form f(x), that is, put in some number x and get something out f(x) (or you could call it y). Calculus looks at how those functions change throughout the domain of the function (differential calculus). It also works in reverse, by looking at your function as a rate of change, we can determine the accumulation of a function (integral calculus). It's important because it allows us to model physical systems and is the backbone for pretty much every (worthwhile) engineering degree. The simplest and most intuitive physical system example is position, velocity, and acceleration. The rate of change (derivative) of position is velocity. The rate of change of position is acceleration. Going the other direction, the accumulation (integral) of acceleration is velocity), and the accumulation of velocity is position. So if I have a function of my velocity over time (say, for instance, your car measures your speed every second) and I integrate this function, it will give me the "accumulation of velocity", or my position, or how far I traveled as a result of my velocity over time.

There are a few levels of calculus, including series/summations/limits, vector calculus, and differential equations that basically build on these foundational concepts.

And as an added bonus: the derivative (rate of change) of acceleration is called "jerk." And if you keep taking derivatives, they are called "snap," "crackle," and "pop."
